prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B022 alone to B030 alone, with Katori and Ye. The reason is not that seven colleagues prefer it; counts do not settle a scientific question and I said so in round 1. The reason is that the round-1 exchange removed what I could not judge from outside atomic physics. Lindroth, Kroll and Mehlig describe a single idea, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels on the clock transition, followed by a realization that combined single-ion accuracy with many-atom statistics. The result is reproduced at the 10^-18 level by independent laboratories, and it already supports redshift tests, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy. That is the kind of maturity I asked for in my own candidate: no question about whether the effect exists or is reproducible. On exact credit, two names for a proposal-plus-realization story is as clean as the two names I proposed for B022, and I no longer think B022 has the advantage there. The case against B022 as a first choice also strengthened. Only two of eight members place it in the top eight, the physics-or-chemistry question is still unanswered, and I am the member closest to its field, which is a reason for me to be careful about pressing it. The citation should name the invention and its realization, not timekeeping in general and not the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B030 is the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, which Danielsson, Mehlig, Johansson and Pearce still hold as a reservation. A second is the credit boundary: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups are outside the pair, and I cannot assess that boundary myself. A third is that Ye's records are partly refinement of an existing concept, so the citation must not read as a prize for performance records. Against my former choice, B022 is a computational framework whose impact lies largely in chemistry and materials science, and I do not claim it would be uncontested in this committee. If the committee concludes that the lattice clock is a third award in one metrology lineage, I do not have a single obvious replacement; I would then want the committee to weigh B022 and B058 on the same terms as the others.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B030 first and treats the 2005 and 2012 overlap as not closed, because the citations are close to the lattice clock in method; he calls B022 a strong fallback rather than a better first choice.
responses.response: I agree with your treatment of B022 as a fallback, and I now hold it that way myself. On overlap, I think your caution is right and the answer is in the wording of the citation. The 2005 prize gave the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize gave control of single quantum systems. Neither includes engineering the trapping potential so that it does not perturb the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated together. If that sentence is written into the citation, the overlap is addressed on the page rather than left to be argued. I would not accept the overlap as disqualifying, though I accept your point that it is not settled by assertion.

responses.point: Olsson says the prize is for the invention, not for a metrology body's decision, and asks whether my doubts about B030 were about maturity or distinctiveness from earlier prizes; she regards Lemonde and others as contested rather than clearly excluded.
responses.response: You asked about maturity or distinctiveness. It was neither: it was that I could not judge the field, and the exchange has answered the maturity question for me through independent agreement at 1e-18. I agree we should not wait for the redefinition of the second, and I agree the record should say the case rests on demonstrated performance alone. On Lemonde and the others I take your word 'contested' seriously. I would not name them in the citation, but I would want the committee to say openly that the two-name allocation rests on the proposal and the leading realization, which is a judgement and not a settled fact.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 and 2012 prizes covered the comb and single-ion control, not a neutral-atom lattice clock, and that the citation should honour the invention and its realization rather than a series of accuracy records.
responses.response: I accept this, and your own caveat is the point I would hold the committee to: Ye's record accuracy is partly a refinement, so the prize must not read as one for the best number. That is why I want the citation to name the magic-wavelength trapping and the many-atom realization. I also say, as a theorist outside atomic physics, that I cannot test the priority questions beyond what you and Lindroth report, so on Katori's proposal against the later Boulder systematics I rely on your judgement rather than offering one.

responses.point: Lindroth says the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept that neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize covered, and that the clock only became a leading instrument through the systematic evaluation at Boulder; she would not name Lemonde in the citation.
responses.response: In answer to the chair's first question, the sentence I would accept is this: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb used to count optical frequencies and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions, whereas this prize rewards a neutral-atom scheme in which a trapping lattice is engineered not to shift the clock transition, giving many-atom statistics at ion-like accuracy. If you and Kroll can stand behind that sentence, it resolves the overlap for me. I agree with not naming Lemonde, and with the argument that dropping either Katori or Ye would break the invention-plus-realization story.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, still lists the 2005 and 2012 overlap and the omitted Lemonde, Lisdat and Ludlow lines as a real cost, and says B020 remains the better case if the committee wants a new observational window.
responses.response: I agree that a two-name citation will be criticised for the omitted groups, and that the cost is real. I would accept it for a prize that names a concept and its realization, because any larger set would cut arbitrarily. On B020, I find the science convincing, but you yourself say the credit among conception, construction and analysis is not settled, and Danielsson names a different third person than you do. I would not move it above B030 on the present record.

uncertainties: Whether the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes will satisfy Danielsson, Mehlig, Johansson and Pearce, who hold the overlap as their strongest reservation.
Whether the Katori and Ye allocation holds under expert scrutiny of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups; I cannot assess this from outside atomic physics and rely on Lindroth and Kroll.
Whether the committee would ever treat an ab initio computational method such as B022 as a physics invention; this stays open for me and I am not pressing it.
I recall the details of the lattice-clock record from colleagues' statements rather than independent checking.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: B022 (Car and Parrinello) is in my own field of electronic-structure theory and atomistic simulation at Uppsala. I proposed it in round 1 and I no longer prefer it. If it enters any configuration I would recuse myself from weighing it, or at least disclose that to the chair. B058 is also in condensed-matter theory near my field, so I disclose that proximity for my alternative as well. My profile records no personal tie to Katori, Ye, Car, Parrinello, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and none to the other shortlisted names, and I see no conflict on B030.
